root_cause: Connection leak introduced in v2.17.4 caused Redis pool exhaustion
root_cause_detail: v2.17.4 added a billing-meta read to the checkout path and a per-worker connection pool. The new code path acquires a Redis client and never returns it to the pool when the billing-meta lookup fails, so within ~14 minutes every worker held max_connections=100 client connections. Pool acquisition then blocked for up to 1s and the API returned 502/503.
resolution: Rolled payment-api back to v2.17.3 and raised the per-worker Redis pool to 150 with a 250ms acquisition timeout; the leak in the v2.17.4 checkout path is fixed in v2.17.5.
contributing_factors: No canary/soak for a cache-pool configuration change on a critical path
Connection lifecycle is not asserted in tests, so a leak ships silently
The service-level runbook's first step is 'restart the pods', which masks a leak rather than fixing it
Pool saturation is only visible in a custom metric, not on the standard dashboard
prevention: Add a pool-saturation SLO alert on redis_connections_active / max_connections
Add a leak detector (open vs returned connections per worker) as a release gate
Require canary soak of 15 minutes for changes touching cache/connection pools
Assert connection release in the checkout test suite
runbook_changes: Move 'inspect Redis client connections per worker' to the top of the payment-api 5xx runbook
Mark 'restart the pods' as a temporary mitigation only, never as remediation for pool exhaustion
Add the deploy-diff step (what changed in the cache/connection path) before restarting anything
lessons: Restarting payment-api pods did not resolve Redis connection-pool exhaustion; it only reset the symptom for under two minutes.
A healthy Redis CPU is expected during pool exhaustion - the client side is the bottleneck, so 'Redis looks fine' is not evidence against it.
Deploy correlation is a lead, not proof: the leak had to be confirmed by the diagnostic (connections opened but never returned).
The cheapest high-information check here was the per-worker connection count, not a restart.
first_checks: what changed in the last 30 minutes for the cache/connection path
whether the client connections are returned to the pool
confirmed_by: redis_connections_active below 90% of max and 5xx back to the 0.4% baseline after rollback
memory_episode: INC-A1 (payment-api, SEV-1): HTTP 503 rose from 0.4% to 31% fourteen minutes after deploying v2.17.4. RedisTimeout plus 'pool active=100 max=100 waiting=37' identified Redis connection-pool exhaustion while Redis CPU stayed normal. Confirmed root cause: a connection leak in the v2.17.4 checkout path drained the per-worker Redis pool. Check first next time: per-worker Redis connection count versus max_connections, and pool acquisition wait time.
memory_service_pattern: payment-api uses a per-worker Redis pool of 100 connections and depends on redis-cache for cart session lookups. The recurring payment-api failure is Redis connection-pool exhaustion: it correlates with recent payment-api releases, always presents as RedisTimeout / 502-503 on /v2/checkout, and never shows elevated Redis CPU. Known dangerous response: restarting pods.
